factProposals.value: Citizens submit requests on a public page (description, location, category, optional contact); each becomes a service request and a work order created by 'public-portal', and the citizen receives a tracking code.
The public can see a work order's status and a plain-language dated history (request received, updated, completed) for published work orders, and for their own request by tracking code.
Staff decide whether a work order is shown publicly (publish/unpublish, audited); new citizen requests are private by default.

Every public submission attempt is logged with time, outcome and the connection's IP address in a staff-only log; X-Forwarded-For is trusted only behind a configured proxy; at most 5 accepted reports per address per hour; the page runs under a strict Content-Security-Policy.

service_requests and public_submission_log tables exist, and work orders have an is_public flag. Citizen contact details and IPs are personal data kept out of every public and outside-system response.
Citizens appear as the system actor 'public-portal' on the work orders their reports create.
Logging IP addresses (the Trust criterion) means storing personal data; the page tells citizens this, and IPs are cleared after a retention period.
The city's records retention rule for submission IP addresses is not known; 90 days is a placeholder.
The STORY-003 brief says it is the last story in the plan; eight stories (STORY-004 to 010 and 012) remain.

decisions.statement: Keep citizen requests private until staff publish them.
decisions.rationale: Unreviewed public submissions can contain anything; staff control what is shown.

decisions.statement: Answer requests for unpublished work orders exactly like missing ones.
decisions.rationale: Prevents probing for hidden records (the unauthorized-access failure path).

decisions.statement: Log every submission attempt, including invalid, unreadable and rate-limited ones.
decisions.rationale: The Trust criterion covers all public submissions, not only accepted ones.

decisions.statement: Take the IP from the connection and trust X-Forwarded-For only behind a configured proxy.
decisions.rationale: Otherwise any client could write any address and avoid both the log and the rate limit.

decisions.statement: Serve the page from a fixed list of files with a strict Content-Security-Policy, and insert server data only as text.
decisions.rationale: No other server file can be reached, and a malicious report cannot inject code into the page.

limitations.statement: If the database is down, a submission cannot be logged or accepted; the citizen gets a 503.
There is no staff screen to publish work orders; publishWorkOrder is called from code.
purgeSubmissionIps() is not run on a schedule.
The public site runs only on a local Node server; GitHub Pages cannot host it because it needs the server.
The rate limit counts accepted reports per address only; shared addresses (e.g. a library) share the limit.
The database schema is created with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS; an existing database file would not get new columns such as is_public without a migration.
